## Learning goals

- Understand how to choose the **right kind of AI system** for a given research task

- Being able to write prompts that are targeted **specifications**

- Know how to **verify** AI output to the standard your term papers are held to

- Being able to **disclose** your use of AI adequately so that it cannot be read as cheating

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Not a goal: knowing which app is currently best.
:::

## How do you use AI at the moment?

::: {.dek}
Two minutes, anonymous. .
:::

- Live poll: **ADD QR CODE**

There are no wrong answers here!

## The productivity evidence points in both directions

::: {.dek}
Careful: "AI makes you faster and
better" is an empirical claim, with a contested evidence base.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Evidence for large gains
:::

- Writing tasks completed **faster and rated better**
  [@noy2023experimental]

- Support agents: more cases, **largest gains for the least experienced** [@brynjolfsson2023generative]

- Consultants better **inside** the model's frontier [@dellacqua2023navigating]
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Evidence for caution
:::

- Same study: **worse** outside it — the "jagged frontier" [@dellacqua2023navigating]

- Experienced developers **slower** — while believing they were faster [@metr2025measuring]

- Self-assessed AI skill: **poor predictor** of performance
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Reliance on AI assistance can _substitute_ for rather than build independent skill, and when the assistance is withdrawn, learners perform worse than if they had developed self-regulated strategies on their own [@darvishi2024impact]
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Honest self reflection is key! AI should neither be demonized nor glorified by default!
:::

## You are accountable for every claim you submit

::: {.dek}
True not only for research; make sure you always check instructor-specific requirements!
:::

- Your **text** is assessed, not your **prompt**

- "The AI said so" is not a reference

- Research or business: **defend what you claim**
    - You must be able to do so **without AI**
    - AI may still generate the claim
    - The demand is verification

::: {.keybox .fragment}
The tool may be new. The standard is not.
:::

## Capabilities, not products {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
02
:::

## The tool list from last year is already wrong

::: {.dek}
Last year, I had sixteen tools mentioned in this lecture. Several no longer
exist, and most of the single-purpose ones have been absorbed into general
assistants.
:::

- AI Tools and products change rapidly
- **Capabilities** are stable: what it does, how you **check** it

- Here: **four capability classes**
  - See the webpage for personal recommendations for each class 

- The skill: **which class**, and **why**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Learn the classes. Products change.
:::

## Four capability classes cover almost everything you need

::: {.dek}
Any one product may combine several of these. Relevant question is never
"which app is best" but "which class am I using right now".
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[A — Conversational assistants]{.caphead}

Generate, restructure, explain and critique text and ideas.
Ungrounded by default.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[B — Grounded search]{.caphead}

Retrieve real sources and cite them. "Deep research" modes chain many
searches into a report.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[C — Document & data analysis]{.caphead}

You supply the material: PDFs, transcripts, datasets. The system reads what
you give it.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[D — Agentic systems]{.caphead}

Plan and execute multi-step work: browse, run code, produce files.
:::
:::

## A and B differ in whether you can check the output

::: {.dek}
Both answer questions in fluent prose. Only one of them leaves you a trail
you can follow back to a source.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A — Conversational assistants
:::

- **Good for** brainstorming, structuring an argument, explaining a method,
  critiquing your own draft

- **Plausible by construction** — fluency ≠ evidence

- No source trail → every claim is **yours to verify**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
B — Grounded search
:::

- **Good for** finding literature, testing whether a claim is established,
  mapping a debate

- **Citations you can follow** — the entire point

- **Strong**: English, open-access, natural sciences

    - **Weak**: books, German, social sciences
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
A citation you have not opened is not a citation.
:::

## C and D differ in how much judgment you delegate

::: {.dek}
In class C you supply the material and keep the reasoning. In class D the
system also decides the steps — which is exactly where it can go wrong
unobserved.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
C — Document & data analysis
:::

- **Good for** a first pass over a long PDF, extracting variables into a
  table, exploring a dataset

- Orientation only — **never** a substitute for reading

- Interview transcripts and firm data are **not yours to upload**
  → section 4 on ethical aspects!
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
D — Agentic systems
:::

- **Good for** multi-step mechanical work with a **checkable** result:
  reformat forty references, run and document an analysis

- You review the **trace**, not only the answer

- Failure mode: confident report, wrong at step three
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Delegate the steps, never the conclusion.
:::

## Every task has a matching class — and a characteristic failure

::: {.dek}
Read the third column as the thing to check before you use the output.
:::

| Task in your term paper | Class | What typically goes wrong |
|:------------------------|:-----:|:--------------------------|
| Narrowing a research question | A | Fluent but unoriginal; converges on the obvious |
| Finding relevant literature | B | Fabricated or mis-attributed references |
| Testing whether a claim is established | B | Confuses "often cited" with "well supported" |
| First pass over a long paper | C | The summary omits the caveat that matters |
| Extracting data from many studies | C | Silent coding errors, spread across the sample |
| Analysing interview transcripts | C | Confidentiality breach; imposed categories |
| Writing and polishing | A | Your voice and your argument flattened |
| R code and data analysis | A / D | The code runs, and answers the wrong question |

: {.tasks}

::: {.source}
Rows 5, 6 and 8 return in lecture 8 (literature reviews), lecture 6
(interviews) and the implementation lab respectively.
:::

::: {.secnum}
Demo

## What to watch in the demo

::: {.dek}
Three questions that apply to any AI output you plan to use in written work.
:::

- **Where does the claim come from?** A source, or only prose?

- **Does the source say it?** Open it — you'd be surprised how often this fails

- **What was left out?** Summaries are confident about what they kept

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Fluency is not evidence.
:::

## Prompting {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
03
:::

## A prompt is a specification, not a wish

::: {.dek}
Most disappointing output is the predictable result of an underspecified
request. Four elements fix the majority of cases.
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[Context]{.caphead}

Who you are, what the work is for, who will read it, what the model should
act as.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Task]{.caphead}

One concrete deliverable, stated as an instruction — not a topic.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Format]{.caphead}

Structure, length, and the sections you expect back.
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Constraints]{.caphead}

What to exclude, which period or region, and what to do when unsure.
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Quality of the prompt → quality of the output.
:::

## The same request, unspecified and specified

::: {.dek}
A real task from this module: you need to narrow a term-paper topic on
remote work.
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Unspecified
:::

- "Give me some research questions about remote work"

- → Ten generic questions, none answerable, all identical to everyone else's
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Specified
:::

- Role, module, level stated

    - **One** deliverable; five questions

    - Each with its **data** and **why it fits 15 pages**

- → Three usable candidates, and why the rest fail
:::
:::

::: {.source}
The full skeleton and a meta-prompt are on the lecture page — do not copy
them off this slide.
:::

## Prompting is a conversation, and worth keeping

::: {.dek}
The first answer is a draft. Treat it the way you treat your own first draft.
:::

- **Iterate**: say what was wrong with the last answer rather than starting
  again

- **Ask it to flag uncertainty** — knowledge vs guess

- **Save what worked** — reusable, and part of your documentation

- Good long-term investment: your own **skill and prompt repo**

- For complex tasks, have the model **draft the prompt** with you first

::: {.keybox .fragment}
A saved prompt is a method. Write it down like one.
:::

## What can go wrong {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
04
:::

## Verification as the key skill

::: {.dek}
Four checks, in order. The first two catch nearly everything that would
embarrass you in an examination.
:::

- **Does the source exist?** Search for it independently, by title

- **Does it say what the answer claims?** Open it and read the relevant page

- **Is it the right source?** Blog post ≠ the study

- **Could I defend this orally?** If not, it does not go in

::: {.keybox .lg .fragment}
Never cite what you have not read.
:::

## Exercise: three citations, one of them invented

::: {.dek}
Groups of three, ten minutes.
:::

::: {.taskbox .fragment}
You will get a short AI-written paragraph with three references.

One is real and correctly used. One is real but says something different.
One does not exist.

Find them, and note **how** you established each verdict.
:::

## Your interview transcripts are not yours to upload

::: {.dek}
This is the rule most likely to cause you actual trouble.
:::

- **Personal data**: consent to interview $\neq$ consent to processing

- Same for **any personal or copyrighted material**

- Anonymise **before** upload

    - Check what the service trains on

    - In doubt: ask **before**

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
If you would not email it to a stranger, do not paste it into a prompt.
:::

## LLMs are never neutral

::: {.dek}
The theory-ladenness of
observation applies to training data too.
:::

- No view from nowhere: output reflects **corpus** and training **choices**

- Biases: **gender, race, age, education** — delicate in hiring and promotion

- Models reproduce the **mainstream** — you should look beyond that

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Ask what a model is likely to under-represent, then go and check.
:::

## The environmental and political-economy questions are unsettled

::: {.dek}
Presented as genuinely open, because it is — and because you will be asked
about it.
:::

- **Energy and water**: efficiency per query up, **total** demand up

- Projections repeatedly revised; credible estimates still disagree

- **Unequal access**: better tools cost money


## Disclosure {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
05
:::

## Undocumented AI use is cheating

::: {.dek}
Not a moral position but a procedural one: unreported assistance makes the
work unassessable.
:::

- **Any** use of AI in coursework for this module must be documented

- **No binding EUF-wide rules** → ask each instructor, every time

- Here additionally: a **paragraph of self-reflection**

::: {.arrow .xl .fragment}
Disclosing costs you nothing. Not disclosing can cost you the module/reputation.
:::

## What a disclosure has to contain

::: {.dek}
Five elements. The fillable template and a worked example are on the lecture
page.
:::

- **Which system**, in which version, accessed when

- **Where** in your work it was used — which sections, which tasks

- **How** you prompted it, in outline

- **How you checked** the output, and what you changed

- **A statement of responsibility**: the text is yours, and you stand behind it

::: {.source}
Template: lecture page → "Documenting and disclosing the use of AI"
(PDF, Word and Markdown).
:::

## Summary & outlook {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
06
:::

## What to take away

- Evidence **real but jagged**: gains, losses, poor self-assessment
  
    - Be aware: **de-skilling** is a risk and adds dependence

- **Four capability classes**, not products: what it does, can you check it

- A prompt is a **specification**; the first answer is a draft

- **Verification** is the skill: never cite what you have not read

- Confidentiality, bias, environment: **central**, not side issues

- **Disclose** everything, and keep your prompts

::: {.keybox .lg .fragment}
Used with judgment, these tools make you better. Used without, they make you
confidently wrong.
:::

## Recap questions

::: {.nonincremental}
- Name the four capability classes and give one research task for each.

- Why is a citation produced by a conversational assistant a different kind
  of object from one produced by a grounded search tool?

- Which four elements make a prompt a specification?

- You are given an AI-written paragraph with three references. Describe how
  you check them.

- Why may you not upload an interview transcript, even anonymised, without
  thinking first?

- In what sense is an LLM "theory-laden"? Relate it to lecture 1.

- What has to appear in an AI disclosure, and why does the self-reflection
  paragraph matter?
:::
